full_judgment:
2. All but two appeals have been preferred without being accompanied by copies of the judgment or order appealed against. In Jail Appeal No. 2098 of 1992, the appellant pleaded guilty of the charge and the Special Tribunal sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years with fine. In Jail Appeal No. 2145 of 1993 the appellant was convicted under section 25B of the Special Powers Act, 1974 by the Special Tribunal No.3, Cox's Bazar and he preferred the appeal out of time by 551 days. In respect of other appeals, the superintendents of jail have communicated the petitions of appeal along with printed forms, (Bangladesh Jail Form No. 27) which contains the name of the convict, the offence, the date of sentence, the sentencing authority, the date of petition for copy of judgment and the date on which the copy was received. The office superintendent of the relevant section of this Court calculated the period of limitation relying upon this form and made endorsement in the order sheet stating that the petitions of appeal were communicated without being accompanied by copies of the judgment. More than ninety percent appeals from the judgments and orders of conviction of the Special Tribunals under Special laws have been communicated out of time as appear from the office notes. The section entertained those appeals and registered as criminal jail appeals. This court by judgment and order dated 27-11-02 dismissed 5 appeals being Criminal Jail Appeal Nos. 483 of 2002, 484 of 2002, 592 of 2002, 593 of 2002 and 595 of 2002 summarily on the ground that the petitions of appeal were not in accordance with law as they were not accompanied by copies of the judgment and order appealed against. Some appeals have been communicated against the judgments of the Magistrates which are not legally maintainable in this Court. 

 3. After the said judgment, it came to our notice that some Division Benches of this Court had admitted appeals preferred under section 420 which were also communicated without being accompanied by copies of the judgment and order appealed against. We had noticed in some cases that the prisoners who were convicted under the Arms Act, 1978, simultaneously moved petitions under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with the copies of the judgment for quashing the conviction and petitions of appeal under section 420 of the Code without accompanying copies of the judgment which were duly admitted which were detected from the lower courts record at the time of hearing of those jail appeals, In some cases the convicts had preferred regular appeals with other co-accused and jail appeals without being accompanied by copies of the judgments appealed against These devices have been being perpetrated in collusion with some corrupt lawyers clerks and touts who have been roaming around the Court premises to prey on these types of prisoners on giving them false assurance of favourable results. Some .Benches of this Court had admitted these appeals by routine orders without application of mind mainly on the reasonings that the convicts were under-privileged prisoners. The moment we came to know that the convicts who were convicted under special laws had been resorting to two forums, one under section 561A of the Code on the ground that they could not prefer appeal within the period of limitation and the other, the petitions of appeal without accompanying the copies of the judgments and even in some cases, they had preferred regular appeals as well as jail appeals, we felt that these practices should be checked in order to avoid conflicting decisions and to curb the multiplication of litigations over the same subject matter. In order to bring uniformity in the decision of this court, we have decided to deal with the matter exhaustively for a future guidance. 

 9. Section 371 of the Code lays down the procedure as to when, how and to whom, the copy of the judgment is to be given. It provides that in certain cases the copy of the judgment be given to the convicted accused free of cost. Even the application for a copy of the judgment need not be stamped. The copy of the judgment referred to in the section is the copy of the judgment of the original court, so that the convict can avail of his right to prefer an appeal with a copy of the judgment. The convict is legally entitled to a copy of the judgment free of cost if he desires to present an appeal and intimates to the jail authority in this regard. Sometimes, the convicts are misled by the ill advice of the courts staffs or advocates clerks of their right of entitlement of a copy of the judgment free of cost. It is not expected that the prisoners are aware of their rights in this regard. The trial Courts have a responsibility in this regard to intimate the convicts of their entitlement of a copy of the judgment in all cases of conviction other than a case under chapter XX of the Code, free of cost after the delivery of the judgment or order so that the convicts, if they desire to appeal and declare that they have no relative, may intimate the superintendent to procure a copy of the judgment. We direct the trial Courts to intimate to all the convicts who are not defended by a lawyer or the convicts though defended by a lawyer intend to prefer jail appeal due to financial or any other cause, of their right of getting copies of the judgment free of cost in order to enable them to present proper appeal within limitation without being misled in the hands of undesiring persons. This direction is given for the interest of justice on consideration of overall socio-economic conditions of the country. A combined reading of these provisions suggest that a convict has a right to appeal against the judgment and order appealed against but subject to the conditions required by the above provisions and also subject to the law of limitation. 

 10. Chapter XIV of Volume I (Part-I) of the Bengal Jail Code, which prescribes the form, the method, the manner of presentation and the facilities that are available to a convict to prepare the petition of appeal within the period of limitation. Sections 599, 600, 603, 604 and 605 of the Jail Code are relevant for our consideration, which are reproduced as follows: 

 These provisions fix the tenor and the responsibility of the officer-in-charge and the superintendent of jail in communicating a petition of appeal to the appellate Court if the convict desires to appeal against the conviction, which should be followed subject to Chapter XXXI of the Code. It is evident from the above provisions that the jail authority is under a legal obligation to render all reasonable facility to the convict as soon as he declares to prefer an appeal from jail. In case of an appeal, which is barred by limitation, the officer-in-charge must endorse on the petition of appeal the reason for not communicating it in time but in most cases we have noticed that no explanation has been given. The jail authorities perform their responsibilities in a callous slipshod manner with the result that most of the appeals are found from the office notes barred by limitation, even in cases of convictions under special laws. The jail authority must record that a convict has an inalienable right to avail all possible facilities for filing an appeal which is enshrined in Chapter XIV of the Jail Code, which request should be promptly attended to so that his appeal can be filed in accordance with law. These less-privileged prisoners should be afforded all co-operations and facilities, which are legally available to them. 

 11. The period of limitation reckons from the date of delivery of the judgment and not from the date of application for copy is made. Where an appeal is filed without a copy of the judgment appealed against there cannot be any scope for calculating the period of limitation and therefore, court cannot exercise its discretionary power to condone the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act. The law of limitation is to be applied strictly in special cases under special laws. When a convict is tried under the Special law, which prescribes a special period of limitation for appeal against an order or judgment by a Special Tribunal or Tribunal or a Bishesh Adalat, as the case may be, in view of section 29 of the Limitation Act, section 5 thereof cannot be applied to exclude the time prescribed by the said Special Law. By reason of Act X of 1922 which came into force on 5th March, 1922 sections 4, 9-18 and 22 of the Limitation Act are applicable to the proceedings under any Special Law insofar as, and to the extent to which they are not expressly excluded by such law. So the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the judgment can be deducted even in an appeal from a conviction under the said Special Law. Section 5 of the Limitation Act is not one of the provisions the application of which is extended by Act X of 1922 to proceedings under the Special Law and therefore, section 5 of the Limitation Act is not applied to such cases. The time requisite for obtaining a copy of the judgment or order appealed against should be deducted under section 12 of the Limitation Act. The application for copy must be made before the period of limitation expires. The convict shall get the benefit of section 12 only if the application for the copy is made at a time when the right to appeal subsists but otherwise not. The time taken in forwarding petition for copies and in transmission of such copies to the jail authority as well as the time taken for the actual preparation of the copies in the office of the court by which the judgment or order was passed is to be included in the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the judgment". In proceedings under special law the appeals must reach the appellate Court in order to prevent their being time-barred. A 'special law' means a law enacted for special cases, in special circumstances, in contradiction to the general rules of the law laid down as applicable generally to all cases with which the general law deals. If a convict is sentenced to imprisonment for life in proceedings under special law his appeal will be dismissed even if the appeal is delayed by one day. It is the responsibility of the superintendent of jail to forthwith apply for a copy of the judgment in BJ. Form No. 27 as soon as the prisoner desires to present an appeal through the jail authority without delay. In some cases we have noticed that the jail authority have not correctly filled up the Bangladesh Jail Forms. The date of the delivery of the judgment and the date for the copy mentioned therein did not tally with the dates mentioned in the judgments. They gave imaginary dates and as a result, the office failed to calculate the period of limitation properly in respect of judgments under special law. The day on which the application for copy has been sent from the jail shall be taken as the date of application for copy. In some cases we have noticed that the jail authorities have taken 7/8 days time in communicating the petitions of appeal after the receipt of the judgments and as a result those appeals have been barred by limitation. The superintendent shall cause his appeal to be written for him by another prisoner if the convict is not able to write the petition. 

 12. In a combined reading of the provisions of law, it is manifest that unless the petition of appeal is accompanied by a copy of the judgment appealed against, the appellate Court will not be in a position to ascertain whether or not the convict pleaded guilty or that the sentence is appealable or that the facts proved constitute an offence or that there are sufficient grounds for interference against the judgment or that it is within the prescribed period of limitation. 

 14. All the above appeals are not legally entertainable, firstly, because the petitions of appeal have not been accompanied by the copies of the judgment appealed against, secondly, almost all the appeals have been preferred beyond the period of limitation against judgments in proceedings under special law and thirdly, some appeals lie to the sessions judge. The convicts have been deprived of access to justice for no fault of their own but because of the laches on the part of the jail authorities. These convicts being less privileged prisoners, they were entitled to avail every reasonable opportunity and facility as per the provisions of the Jail Code but they had been denied of getting justice for the acts or omissions of the persons who were under a legal obligation to render all reasonable assistance to them in accordance with the Jail Code. We hope that there shall not be any further violation of the Jail Code in respect of the less privileged prisoners who intend to present jail appeals through the jail authorities. 

 (e) if a petition of appeal is late as to render it impossible to reach the appellate Court within the prescribed period of limitation, the officer- in-charge shall endorse on the petition the reason for not communicating it in time.
